newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Mounties say not stymied in Bre-X case.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Mounties say not stymied in Bre-X case.

text.p: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police moved on Wednesday to dispel reports that its worldwide investigation into the Bre-X Minerals Ltd. Indonesian gold scandal had sputtered and was coming up dry.

The two top Mounties involved in the case, which began in early May after Bre-X's Busang gold deposit was revealed as the world's biggest-ever mining fraud, told a news conference that the investigation was proceeding as expected.

"The RCMP have not run into a brick wall. We are not stumbling," Chief Supt. Rod MacKay said. "Things are going quite well. We are progressing as we felt we would be at this stage of the investigation."
The police officials, however, offered few specifics on the epic investigation, which has so far stretched from Canada to Indonesia, the Philippines and Australia.
Bre-X, its management and some Canadian and U.S. brokerages have been named in a series of shareholder suits tied to the scandal.
The RCMP declined to speculate on when charges would be laid and against whom.

"There are a number of interviews that have to be conducted," MacKay said. "We have copious amounts of documents and files that have to be gone through by our analysts and by our forensic investigators. So there's lots to do."

The Toronto Globe and Mail Newspaper reported on Tuesday that the Mounties were being frustrated in their efforts to find out who was behind the scandal, which saw investor equity in Calgary-based Bre-X -- once valued at up to C$6 billion ($4.3 billion) -- reduced to worthless paper.

Quoting an RCMP staff sergeant, the Globe and Mail also said police had been unable to interview John Felderhof, Bre-X's since-fired chief of exploration, who has been at his posh estate in the Cayman Islands since the scandal rocked the world's mining industry.
But MacKay said on Wednesday that investigators had not yet tried to interview Felderhof.
"In any investigation, you must go out and gather evidence, interview people and have a case prepared, whether it's Mr. Felderhof or anyone," he said.
"We are at the stage of investigating, interviewing people and gathering evidence. We are not yet at the stage to approach or arrest anyone."
Further, MacKay said there had been no attempt to extradite Felderhof, who with Bre-X Chief Executive David Walsh and chief geologist Michael de Guzman was one of the key figures in the Busang saga.

In March, de Guzman was reported dead, apparently of suicide, after falling from a helicopter en route to Busang to meet with officials from Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. . New Orleans-based Freeport was conducting due diligence of the property in expectation of becoming Bre-X's partner in its development.

Although questions have lingered since the incident over whether de Guzman committed suicide or was murdered, and if the body found in the dense jungle was indeed his, the Mounties said they believed earlier official conclusions.

"We're quite satisfied in the investigation that was done in Indonesia as well as a subsequent investigation by the Philippine authorities," said Insp. Peter Macaulay, who was recently installed as the top investigator in the case.
"We are satisfied that Michael de Guzman did commit suicide and that the body recovered was that of Michael de Guzman," Macaulay said.
The police also said they had not restricted Walsh's ability to leave Canada and that Bre-X officials were cooperating with investigators.
